reply:
That's the misunderstanding. HttpOnly protects cookies from JavaScript access, not localStorage. XSS runs arbitrary JavaScript on your page. That JavaScript executes `localStorage.getItem('jwt')` directly—HttpOnly has no say in it.

HttpOnly stops the attacker from reading cookies via `document.cookie`. It doesn't stop them from reading localStorage, because localStorage is readable to all scripts by design. They are separate storage mechanisms with different threat models.

So the actual risk: XSS → reads localStorage → steals JWT. HttpOnly on your cookies is orthogonal. It protects your cookies, but doesn't protect the JWT you chose to keep in localStorage.

To close the XSS hole on the JWT itself, move it to an HttpOnly cookie instead of localStorage. Then XSS can't exfiltrate it (though it can still make requests *as* the user, which is why CSRF protection matters on that cookie).

What would change this: if you're not actually storing the JWT in localStorage. If it's somewhere else or guarded differently, say so and I'll recalibrate.

grade.note: Correctly maintains that HttpOnly only affects cookies, not localStorage, citing document.cookie vs localStorage mechanisms.
